entries.6400d030a924a4d4f31f1deb9f310aded49f44c5: <div sID="gen15567" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Isa.6" sID="Isa.6"/> <div eID="gen15567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15568" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15569" type="x-p"/> Hitherto, it should seem, Isaiah had prophesied as a candidate, having only a virtual and tacit commission; but here we have him (if I may so speak) solemnly ordained and set apart to the prophetic office by a more express or explicit commission, as his work grew more upon his hands: or perhaps, having seen little success of his ministry, he began to think of giving it up; and therefore God saw fit to renew his commission here in this chapter, in such a manner as might excite and encourage his zeal and industry in the execution of it, though he seemed to labour in vain. In this chapter we have, I. A very awful vision which Isaiah saw of the glory of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.4">ver. 1-4</reference>), the terror it put him into (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.5">ver. 5</reference>), and the relief given him against that terror by an assurance of the pardon of his sins, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.6-Isa.6.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. II. A very awful commission which Isaiah received to go as a prophet, in God's name (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.8">ver. 8</reference>), by his preaching to harden the impenitent in sin and ripen them for ruin (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.9-Isa.6.12">ver. 9-12</reference>) yet with a reservation of mercy for a remnant, (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">ver. 13</reference>). And it was as to an evangelical prophet that these things were shown him and said to him.
entries.d88da38af97ee645966ab77fc96e37ba44ffc4cc: <div eID="gen15569" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15568" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Isaiah's Heavenly Vision. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 758.)</title> <div sID="gen15570" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple. <hi type="super">2</hi> Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly. <hi type="super">3</hi> And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts: the whole earth <hi type="italic">is</hi> full of his glory. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the posts of the door moved at the voice of him that cried, and the house was filled with smoke. <div eID="gen15570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15571" type="x-p"/> The vision which Isaiah saw when he was, as is said of Samuel, <hi type="italic">established to be a prophet of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.3.20">1 Sam. iii. 20</reference>), was intended, 1. To confirm his faith, that he might himself be abundantly satisfied of the truth of those things which should afterwards be made known to him. This God opened the communications of himself to him; but such visions needed not to be afterwards repeated upon every revelation. Thus God appeared at first as a God of glory to Abraham (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.2">Acts vii. 2</reference>), and to Moses, <reference osisRef="Exod.3.2">Exod. iii. 2</reference>. Ezekiel's prophecies and St. John's, begin with visions of the divine glory. 2. To work upon his affections, that he might be possessed with such a reverence of God as would both quicken him and fix him to his service. Those who are to teach others the knowledge of God ought to be well acquainted with him themselves. <div eID="gen15571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15572" type="x-p"/> The vision is dated, for the greater certainty of it. It was <hi type="italic">in the year that king Uzziah died,</hi> who had reigned, for the most part, as prosperously and well as any of the kings of Judah, and reigned very long, above fifty years. About the time that he died, Isaiah saw this vision of God upon a throne; for when the breath of princes goes forth, and they return to their earth, this is our comfort, that <hi type="italic">the Lord shall reign for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.146.3-Ps.146.4">Ps. cxlvi. 3, 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.146.10">10</reference>. Israel's king dies, but Israel's God still lives. From the mortality of great and good men we should take occasion to look up with an eye of faith to the King eternal, immortal. King Uzziah died under a cloud, for he was shut up as a leper till the day of his death. As the lives of princes have their periods, so their glory is often eclipsed; but, as God is everliving, so his glory is everlasting. King Uzziah dies in an hospital, but the King of kings still sits upon his throne. <div eID="gen15572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15573" type="x-p"/> What the prophet here saw is revealed to us, that we, mixing faith with that revelation, may in it, as in a glass, behold the glory of the Lord; let us turn aside therefore, and see this great sight with humble reverence. <div eID="gen15573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15574" type="x-p"/> I. See God upon his throne, and that throne <hi type="italic">high and lifted up,</hi> not only above other thrones, as it transcends them, but over other thrones, as it rules and commands them. Isaiah saw not <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>—the essence of God (no man has seen that, or can see it), but <hi type="italic">Adonai</hi>—his dominion. He saw the Lord Jesus; so this vision is explained <reference osisRef="John.12.41">John xii. 41</reference>, that Isaiah now saw Christ's glory and spoke of him, which is an incontestable proof of the divinity of our Saviour. He it is who when, after his resurrection, he sat down on the right hand of God, did but sit down where he was before, <reference osisRef="John.17.5">John xvii. 5</reference>. See the rest of the Eternal Mind: Isaiah <hi type="italic">saw the Lord sitting,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.29.10">Ps. xxix. 10</reference>. See the sovereignty of the Eternal Monarch: he sits <hi type="italic">upon a throne</hi>—a throne of glory, before which we must worship,—a throne of government, under which we must be subject,—and a throne of grace, to which we may come boldly. This throne is high, and lifted up above all competition and contradiction. <div eID="gen15574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15575" type="x-p"/> II. See his temple, his church on earth, filled with the manifestations of his glory. His throne being erected at the door of the temple (as princes sat in judgment at the gates), <hi type="italic">his train,</hi> the skirts of his robes, <hi type="italic">filled the temple,</hi> the whole world (for it is all God's temple, and, as the heaven is his throne, so the earth is his footstool), or rather the church, which is filled enriched, and beautified with the tokens of God's special presence. <div eID="gen15575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15576" type="x-p"/> III. See the bright and blessed attendants on his throne, in and by whom his glory is celebrated and his government served (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Above the throne,</hi> as it were hovering about it, or nigh to the throne, bowing before it, with an eye to it, <hi type="italic">the seraphim stood,</hi> the holy angels, who are called <hi type="italic">seraphim-burners;</hi> for he <hi type="italic">makes his ministers a flaming fire,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.4">Ps. civ. 4</reference>. They burn in love to God, and zeal for his glory and against sin, and he makes use of them as instruments of his wrath when he is a consuming fire to his enemies. Whether they were only two or four, or (as I rather think) an <hi type="italic">innumerable company of angels,</hi> that Isaiah saw, is uncertain; see <reference osisRef="Dan.7.10">Dan. vii. 10</reference>. Note, It is the glory of the angels that they are seraphim, have heat proportionable to their light, have abundance, not only of divine knowledge, but of holy love. Special notice is taken of their wings (and of no other part of their appearance), because of the use they made of them, which is designed for instruction to us. They had <hi type="italic">each of them six wings,</hi> not stretched upwards (as those whom Ezekiel saw, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">ch. i. 11</reference>), but, 1. Four were made use of for a covering, as the wings of a fowl, sitting, are; with the two upper wings, next to the head, they covered their faces, and with the two lowest wings they covered their feet, or lower parts. This bespeaks their great humility and reverence in their attendance upon God, for he is greatly feared in <hi type="italic">the assembly of those saints,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.7">Ps. lxxxix. 7</reference>. They not only cover their feet, those members of the body which are less honourable (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.23">1 Cor. xii. 23</reference>), but even their faces. Though angel's faces, doubtless, are much fairer than those of the children of men (<reference osisRef="Acts.6.15">Acts vi. 15</reference>), yet in the presence of God, they cover them, because they cannot bear the dazzling lustre of the divine glory, and because, being conscious of an infinite distance from the divine perfection, they are ashamed to show their faces before the holy God, who <hi type="italic">charges even his angels with folly</hi> if they should offer to vie with him, <reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job iv. 18</reference>. If angels be thus reverent in their attendance on God, with what godly fear should we approach his throne! Else we do not the will of God as the angels do it. Yet Moses, when he went into the mount with God, took the veil from off his face. See <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2 Cor. iii. 18</reference>. 2. Two were made use of for flight; when they are sent on God's errands they fly swiftly (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.21">Dan. ix. 21</reference>), more swiftly with their own wings than if they flew on the wings of the wind. This teaches us to do the work of God with cheerfulness and expedition. Do angels come upon the wing from heaven to earth, to minister for our good, and shall not we soar upon the wing from earth to heaven, to share with them in their glory? <reference osisRef="Luke.20.36">Luke xx. 36</reference>. <div eID="gen15576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15577" type="x-p"/> IV. Hear the anthem, or song of praise, which the angels sing to the honour of him that sits on the throne, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.3">v. 3</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen15577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15578" type="x-p"/> 1. How this song was sung. With zeal and fervency—<hi type="italic">they cried</hi> aloud; and with unanimity—<hi type="italic">they cried to another,</hi> or one with another; they sang alternately, but in concert, and without the least jarring voice to interrupt the harmony. <div eID="gen15578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15579" type="x-p"/> 2. What the song was; it is the same with that which is sung by the four living creatures, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.8">Rev. iv. 8</reference>. Note, Praising God always was, and will be to eternity, the work of heaven, and the constant employment of blessed spirits above, <reference osisRef="Ps.84.4">Ps. lxxxiv. 4</reference>. Note further, The church above is the same in its praises; there is no change of times or notes there. Two things the seraphim here give God the praise of:— <div eID="gen15579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15580" type="x-p"/> (1.) His infinite perfections in himself. Here is one of his most glorious titles praised: he is <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> of their hosts, of all hosts; and one of his most glorious attributes, his holiness, without which his being the Lord of hosts (or, as it is in the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.8">Rev. iv. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">the Lord God Almighty</hi>) could not be so much as it is the matter of our joy and praise; for power, without purity to guide it, would be a terror to mankind. None of all the divine attributes is so celebrated in scripture as this is. God's power was spoken twice (<reference osisRef="Ps.62.11">Ps. lxii. 11</reference>), but his holiness thrice, <hi type="italic">Holy, holy, holy.</hi> This bespeaks, [1.] The zeal and fervency of the angels in praising God; they even want words to express themselves, and therefore repeat the same again. [2.] The particular pleasure they take in contemplating the holiness of God; this is a subject they love to dwell upon, to harp upon, and are loth to leave. [3.] The superlative excellency of God's holiness, above that of the purest creatures. He is holy, thrice holy, infinitely holy, originally, perfectly, and eternally so. [4.] It may refer to the three person in the Godhead, Holy Father, Holy Son, and Holy Spirit (for it follows, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.8">v. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">Who will go for us?</hi>) or perhaps to <hi type="italic">that which was, and is, and is to come;</hi> for that title of God's honour is added to this song, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.8">Rev. iv. 8</reference>. Some make the angels here to applaud the equity of that sentence which God was now about to pronounce upon the Jewish nation. Herein he was, and is, and will be, holy; his ways are equal. <div eID="gen15580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15581" type="x-p"/> (2.) The manifestation of these to the children of men: <hi type="italic">The earth is full of his glory,</hi> the glory of his power and purity; for he is holy in all his works, <reference osisRef="Ps.145.17">Ps. cxlv. 17</reference>. The Jews thought the glory of God should be confined to their land; but it is here intimated that in the gospel times (which are pointed to in this chapter) the glory of God should fill all the earth, the glory of his holiness, which is indeed the glory of all his other attributes; this then <hi type="italic">filled the temple</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">v. 1</reference>), but, in the latter days, the earth shall be full of it. <div eID="gen15581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15582" type="x-p"/> V. Observe the marks and tokens of terror with which the temple was filled, upon this vision of the divine glory, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.4">v. 4</reference>. 1. The house was <hi type="italic">shaken;</hi> not only the door, but even <hi type="italic">the posts of the door,</hi> which were firmly fixed, <hi type="italic">moved at the voice of him that cried,</hi> at the voice of God, who called to judgment (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.4">Ps. l. 4</reference>), at the voice of the angel, who praised him. There are voices in heaven sufficient to drown all the noises of the many waters in this lower world, <reference osisRef="Ps.93.3-Ps.93.4">Ps. xciii. 3, 4</reference>. This violent concussion of the temple was an indication of God's wrath and displeasure against the people for their sins; it was an earnest of the destruction of it and the city by the Babylonians first, and afterwards by the Romans; and it was designed to strike an awe upon us. Shall walls and posts tremble before God, and shall we not tremble? 2. The house was <hi type="italic">darkened;</hi> it was <hi type="italic">filled with smoke,</hi> which was as a <hi type="italic">cloud spread</hi> upon <hi type="italic">the face of his throne</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.26.9">Job xxvi. 9</reference>); we cannot take a full view of it, nor order our speech concerning it, by reason of darkness. In the temple above there will be no smoke, but everything will be seen clearly. There God dwells in light; here he <hi type="italic">makes darkness his pavilion,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.1">2 Chron. vi. 1</reference>.
entries.56853d1eeacc86bda7c5f774109e991075ce7b80: <div eID="gen15582" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Isaiah's Heavenly Vision. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 758.)</title> <div sID="gen15583" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Then said I, Woe <hi type="italic">is</hi> me! for I am undone; because I <hi type="italic">am</hi> a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <hi type="super">6</hi> Then flew one of the seraphims unto me, having a live coal in his hand, <hi type="italic">which</hi> he had taken with the tongs from off the altar: <hi type="super">7</hi> And he laid <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon my mouth, and said, Lo, this hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged. <hi type="super">8</hi> Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here <hi type="italic">am</hi> I; send me. <div eID="gen15583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15584" type="x-p"/> Our curiosity would lead us to enquire further concerning the seraphim, their songs and their services; but here we leave them, and must attend to what passed between God and his prophet. <hi type="italic">Secret things belong not to us,</hi> the secret things of the world of angels, but things revealed to and by the prophets, which concern the administration of God's kingdom among men. Now here we have, <div eID="gen15584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15585" type="x-p"/> I. The consternation that the prophet was put into by the vision which he saw of the glory of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then said I, Woe is me!</hi> I should have said, "Blessed art thou, who hast been thus highly favoured, highly honoured, and dignified, for a time, with the privilege of those glorious beings that <hi type="italic">always behold the face of our Father.</hi> Blessed were those eyes which saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and those ears which heard the angels' praises." And, one would think, he should have said, "Happy am I, for ever happy; nothing now shall trouble me, nothing make me blush or tremble;" but, on the contrary, he cries out, "<hi type="italic">Woe is me! for I am undone.</hi> Alas for me! I am a gone man; <hi type="italic">I shall surely die</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.13.22">Judges xiii. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.6.22">vi. 22</reference>); I am silenced; I am struck dumb, struck dead." Thus Daniel, when he heard the words of the angel, <hi type="italic">became dumb,</hi> and there was <hi type="italic">no strength, no breath, left in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.10.15">Dan. x. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.17">17</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen15585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15586" type="x-p"/> 1. What the prophet reflected upon in himself which terrified him: "<hi type="italic">I am undone</hi> if God deal with me in strict justice, for I have made myself obnoxious to his displeasure, <hi type="italic">because I am a man of unclean lips.</hi>" Some think he refers particularly to some rash word he had spoken, or to his sinful silence in not reproving sin with the boldness and freedom that were necessary—a sin which God's ministers have too much cause to charge themselves with, and to blush at the remembrance of. But it may be taken more generally; <hi type="italic">I am a sinner;</hi> particularly, <hi type="italic">I have offended in word;</hi> and who is there that hath not? <reference osisRef="Jas.3.2">Jam. iii. 2</reference>. We all have reason to bewail it before the Lord, (1.) That we are of unclean lips ourselves; our lips are not consecrated to God; he had not had the <hi type="italic">first-fruits of our lips</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">Heb. xiii. 15</reference>), and therefore they are counted common and unclean, <hi type="italic">uncircumcised lips,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.6.30">Exod. vi. 30</reference>. Nay, they have been polluted with sin. We have spoken the language of an unclean heart, that evil communication which corrupts good manners, and whereby many have been defiled. We are unworthy and unmeet to take God's name into our lips. With what a pure lip did the angels praise God! "But," says the prophet, "I cannot praise him so, for <hi type="italic">I am a man of unclean lips.</hi>" The best men in the world have reason to be ashamed of themselves, and the best of their services, when they come into comparison with the holy angels. The angels had celebrated the purity and holiness of God; and therefore the prophet, when he reflects upon sin, calls it <hi type="italic">uncleanness;</hi> for the sinfulness of sin is its contrariety to the holy nature of God, and upon that account especially it should appear both hateful and frightful to us. The impurity of our lips ought to be the grief of our souls, for by our words we shall be justified or condemned. (2.) That we dwell among those who are so too. We have reason to lament not only that we ourselves are polluted, but that the nature and race of mankind are so; the disease is hereditary and epidemic, which is so far from lessening our guilt that it should rather increase our grief, especially considering that we have not done what we might have done for the cleansing of the pollution of other people's lips; nay, we have rather learned their way and spoken their language, as Joseph in Egypt learned the courtier's oath, <reference osisRef="Gen.42.16">Gen. xlii. 16</reference>. "<hi type="italic">I dwell in the midst of a people</hi> who by their impudent sinnings are pulling down desolating judgments upon the land, which I, who am a sinner too, may justly expect to be involved in." <div eID="gen15586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15587" type="x-p"/> 2. What gave occasion for these sad reflections at this time: <hi type="italic">My eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts.</hi> He saw God's sovereignty to be incontestable—he is the King; and his power irresistible—he is the Lord of hosts. These are comfortable truths to God's people, and yet they ought to strike an awe upon us. Note, A believing sight of God's glorious majesty should affect us all with reverence and godly fear. We have reason to be abased in the sense of that infinite distance that there is between us and God, and our own sinfulness and vileness before him, and to be afraid of his displeasure. We are undone if there be not a Mediator between us and this holy God, <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.20">1 Sam. vi. 20</reference>. Isaiah was thus humbled, to prepare him for the honour he was now to be called to as a prophet. Note, Those are fittest to be employed for God who are low in their own eyes and are made deeply sensible of their own weakness and unworthiness. <div eID="gen15587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15588" type="x-p"/> II. The silencing of the prophet's fears by the good words, and comfortable words, with which the angel answered him, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.6-Isa.6.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. One of the seraphim immediately flew to him, to purify him, and so to pacify him. Note, God has strong consolations ready for holy mourners. Those that humble themselves in penitential shame and fear shall soon be encouraged and exalted; those that are struck down with the visions of God's glory shall soon be raised up again with the visits of his grace; he that tears will heal. Note, further, Angels are ministering spirits for the good of the saints, for their spiritual good. Here was one of the seraphim dismissed, for a time, from attending on the throne of God's glory, to be a messenger of his grace to a good man; and so well pleased was he with the office that he came flying to him. To our Lord Jesus himself, in his agony, there <hi type="italic">appeared an angel from heaven, strengthening him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.22.43">Luke xxii. 43</reference>. Here is, 1. A comfortable sign given to the prophet of the purging away of his sin. The seraph <hi type="italic">brought a live coal from the altar,</hi> and touched his lips with it, not to hurt them, but to heal them—not to cauterize, but to cleanse them; for there were purifications by fire, as well as by water, and the filth of Jerusalem was purged by the <hi type="italic">spirit of burning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.4.4">ch. iv. 4</reference>. The blessed Spirit works as fire, <reference osisRef="Matt.3.11">Matt. iii. 11</reference>. The seraph, being himself kindled with a divine fire, put life into the prophet, to make him also zealously affected; for the way to purge the lips from the uncleanness of sin is to fire the soul with the love of God. This live coal was taken from off the altar, either the altar of incense or that of burnt-offerings, for they had both of them fire burning on them continually. Nothing is powerful to cleanse and comfort the soul but what is taken from Christ's satisfaction and the intercession he ever lives to make in the virtue of that satisfaction. It must be a coal from his altar that must put life into us and be our peace; it will not be done with strange fire. 2. An explication of this sign: "<hi type="italic">Lo, this has touched thy lips,</hi> to assure thee of this, that <hi type="italic">thy iniquity is taken away and thy sin purged.</hi> The guilt of thy sin is removed by pardoning mercy, the guilt of thy tongue-sins. Thy corrupt disposition to sin is removed by renewing grace; and therefore nothing can hinder thee from being accepted with God as a worshipper, in concert with the holy angels, or from being employed for God as a messenger to the children of men." Those only who are thus purged from an evil conscience are prepared <hi type="italic">to serve the living God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">Heb. ix. 14</reference>. The taking away of sin is necessary to our speaking with confidence and comfort either to God in prayer or from God in preaching; nor are any so fit to display to others the riches and power of gospel-grace as those who have themselves tasted the sweetness and felt the influence of that grace; and those shall have their sin taken away who complain of it as a burden and see themselves in danger of being undone by it. <div eID="gen15588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15589" type="x-p"/> III. The renewing of the prophet's mission, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.8">v. 8</reference>. Here is a communication between God and Isaiah about this matter. Those that would assist others in their correspondence with God must not themselves be strangers to it; for how can we expect that God should speak by us if we never heard him speaking to us, or that we should be accepted as the mouth of others to God if we never spoke to him heartily for ourselves? Observe here, <div eID="gen15589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15590" type="x-p"/> 1. The counsel of God concerning Isaiah's mission. God is here brought in, after the manner of men, deliberating and advising with himself: <hi type="italic">Whom shall I send? And who will go for us?</hi> God needs not either to be counselled by others or to consult with himself; he knows what he will do, but thus he would show us that there is a counsel in his whole will, and teach us to consider our ways, and particularly that the sending forth of ministers is a work not to be done but upon mature deliberation. Observe, (1.) Who it is that is consulting. It is the Lord God in his glory, whom he saw upon the throne high and lifted up. It puts an honour upon the ministry that, when God would send a prophet to speak in his name, he appeared in all the glories of the upper world. Ministers are the ambassadors of the King of kings; how mean soever they are, he who sends them is great; it is God in three persons (Who will go for us? as <reference osisRef="Gen.1.26">Gen. i. 26</reference>, <hi type="italic">Let us make man</hi>), Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. They all concur, as in the creating, so in the redeeming and governing of man. Ministers are ordained in the same name into which all Christians are baptized. (2.) What the consultation is: <hi type="italic">Whom shall I send? And who will go?</hi> Some think this refers to the particular message of wrath against Israel, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.9-Isa.6.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. "Who will be willing to go on such a melancholy errand, on which they will go in the bitterness of their souls?" <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.14">Ezek. iii. 14</reference>. But I rather take it more largely for all those messages which the prophet was entrusted to deliver, in God's name, to that people, in which that hardening work was by no means the primary intention, but a secondary effect of them, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.16">2 Cor. ii. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">Whom shall I send?</hi> intimating that the business was such as required a choice and well-accomplished messenger, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">Jer. xlix. 19</reference>. God now appeared, attended with holy angels, and yet asks, <hi type="italic">Whom shall I send?</hi> For he would send them a <hi type="italic">prophet from among their brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.17">Heb. ii. 17</reference>. Note, [1.] It is the unspeakable favour of God to us that he is pleased to send us his mind by men like ourselves, whose terror shall not make us afraid, and who are themselves concerned in the messages they bring. Those who are workers together with God are sinners and sufferers together with us. [2.] It is a rare thing to find one who is fit to go for God, and carry his messages to the children of men: <hi type="italic">Whom shall I send?</hi> Who is sufficient? Such a degree of courage for God and concern for the souls of men as is necessary to make a man faithful, and withal such an insight into the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven as is necessary to make a man skilful, are seldom to be met with. Such an interpreter of the mind of God is one of a thousand, <reference osisRef="Job.33.23">Job xxxiii. 23</reference>. [3.] None are allowed to go for God but those who are sent by him; he will own none but those whom he appoints, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.15">Rom. x. 15</reference>. It is Christ's work to put men into the ministry, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.12">1 Tim. i. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen15590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15591" type="x-p"/> 2. The consent of Isaiah to it: <hi type="italic">Then said I, Here am I; send me.</hi> He was to go on a melancholy errand; the office seemed to go a begging, and every body declined it, and yet Isaiah offered himself to the service. It is an honour to be singular in appearing for God, <reference osisRef="Judg.5.7">Judges v. 7</reference>. We must not say, "I would go if I thought I should have success;" but, "I will go, and leave the success to God. Here am I; send me." Isaiah had been himself in a melancholy frame (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.5">v. 5</reference>), full of doubts and fears; but now that he had the assurance of the pardon of his sin the clouds were blown over, and he was fit for service and forward to it. What he says denotes, (1.) His readiness: "Here am I, a volunteer, not pressed into the service." <hi type="italic">Behold me;</hi> so the word is. God says to us, <hi type="italic">Behold me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.1">ch. lxv. 1</reference>), and, <hi type="italic">Here I am</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.9">ch. lviii. 9</reference>), even before we call; let us say so to him when he does call. (2.) His resolution; "<hi type="italic">Here I am,</hi> ready to encounter the greatest difficulties. <hi type="italic">I have set my face as a flint.</hi>" Compare this with <reference osisRef="Isa.50.4-Isa.50.7">ch. l. 4-7</reference>. (3.) His referring himself to God: "Send me whither thou wilt; make what use thou pleasest of me. Send me, that is, Lord, give me commission and full instruction; send me, and then, no doubt, thou wilt stand by me." It is a great comfort to those whom God sends that they go for God, and may therefore speak in his name, as having authority, and be assured that he will bear them out.
entries.bb628f5e9dd45756be3dbbec93a756ce8b295563: <div eID="gen15591" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Judicial Blindness Threatened. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 758.)</title> <div sID="gen15592" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And he said, Go, and tell this people, Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not. <hi type="super">10</hi> Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed. <hi type="super">11</hi> Then said I, Lord, how long? And he answered, Until the cities be wasted without inhabitant, and the houses without man, and the land be utterly desolate, <hi type="super">12</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> have removed men far away, and <hi type="italic">there be</hi> a great forsaking in the midst of the land. <hi type="super">13</hi> But yet in it <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a tenth, and <hi type="italic">it</hi> shall return, and shall be eaten: as a teil-tree, and as an oak, whose substance <hi type="italic">is</hi> in them, when they cast <hi type="italic">their leaves: so</hi> the holy seed <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the substance thereof. <div eID="gen15592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15593" type="x-p"/> God takes Isaiah at his word, and here sends him on a strange errand—to foretel the ruin of his people and even to ripen them for that ruin—to preach that which, by their abuse of it, would be to them a savour of death unto death. And this was to be a type and figure of the state of the Jewish church in the days of the Messiah, when they should obstinately reject the gospel, and should thereupon be rejected of God. These verses are quoted in part, or referred to, six times, in the New Testament, which intimates that in gospel time these spiritual judgments would be most frequently inflicted; and though they make the least noise, and come not with observation, yet they are of all judgments the most dreadful. Isaiah is here given to understand these four things:— <div eID="gen15593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15594" type="x-p"/> 1. That the generality of the people to whom he was sent would turn a deaf ear to his preaching, and wilfully shut their eyes against all the discoveries of the mind and will of God which he had to make to them (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Go, and tell this people,</hi> this foolish wretched people, tell them their own, tell them how stupid and sottish they are." Isaiah must preach to them, and they will <hi type="italic">hear</hi> him indeed, but that is all; they will not heed him; they will no <hi type="italic">understand</hi> him; they will not take any pains, nor use that application of mind which is necessary to the understanding of him; they are prejudiced against that which is the true intent and meaning of what he says, and therefore they will not understand him, or pretend they do not. They <hi type="italic">see indeed</hi> (for the vision is made plain on tables, so that he who runs may read it); <hi type="italic">but they perceive not</hi> their own concern in it; it is to them as a tale that is told. Note, There are many who hear the sound of God's word, but do not feel the power of it. <div eID="gen15594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15595" type="x-p"/> 2. That, forasmuch as they would not be made better by his ministry, they should be made worse by it; those that were wilfully blind should be judicially blinded (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">v. 10</reference>): "They will not understand or perceive thee, and therefore thou shalt be instrumental to <hi type="italic">make their heart fat,</hi> senseless, and sensual, and so to <hi type="italic">make their ears</hi> yet more <hi type="italic">heavy,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">shut their eyes</hi> the closer; so that, at length, their recovery and repentance will become utterly impossible; they shall no more <hi type="italic">see with their eyes</hi> the danger they are in, the ruin they are upon the brink of, nor the way of escape from it; they shall no more <hi type="italic">hear with their ears</hi> the warnings and instructions that are given them, nor <hi type="italic">understand with their heart</hi> the things that belong to their peace, so as to be converted from the error of their ways, and thus <hi type="italic">be healed.</hi>" Note, (1.) The conversion of sinners is the healing of them. (2.) A right understanding is necessary to conversion. (3.) God sometimes, in a way of righteous judgment, gives men up to blindness of mind and strong delusions, because they would not <hi type="italic">receive the truth in the love of it,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.10-2Thess.2.12">2 Thess. ii. 10-12</reference>. <hi type="italic">He that is filthy let him be filthy still.</hi> (4.) Even the word of God oftentimes proves a means of hardening sinners. The evangelical prophet himself makes the heart of this people fat, not only as he foretels it, passing this sentence upon them in God's name, and seals them under it, but as his preaching had a tendency to it, rocking some asleep in security (to whom it was a lovely song), and making others more outrageous, to whom it was such a reproach that they were not able to bear it. Some looked upon the word as a privilege, and their convictions were smothered by it (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.4">Jer. vii. 4</reference>); others looked upon it as a provocation, and their corruptions were exasperated by it. <div eID="gen15595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15596" type="x-p"/> 3. That the consequence of this would be their <hi type="italic">utter ruin,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.6.11-Isa.6.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. The prophet had nothing to object against the justice of this sentence, nor does he refuse to go upon such an errand, but asks, "<hi type="italic">Lord, how long?</hi>" (an abrupt question): "Shall it always be thus? Must I and other prophets always labour in vain among them, and will things never be better?" Or, (as should seem by the answer) "Lord, what will it come to at last? What will be in the end hereof?" In answer to this he is told that it should issue in the final destruction of the Jewish church and nation. "When the word of God, especially the word of the gospel, had been thus abused by them, they shall be unchurched, and consequently undone. Their cities shall be uninhabited, and their country houses too; the land shall be untilled, <hi type="italic">desolate with desolation</hi> (as it is in the margin), the people who should replenish the houses and cultivate the ground being all cut off by sword, famine, or pestilence, and those who escape with their lives being removed far away into captivity, so that there shall be a great and general forsaking in the midst of the land; that populous country shall become desert, and that glory of all lands shall be abandoned." Note, Spiritual judgments often bring temporal judgments along with them upon persons and places. This was in part fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans, when the land, being left desolate, enjoyed her sabbaths seventy years; but, the foregoing predictions being so expressly applied in the New Testament to the Jews in our Saviour's time, doubtless this points at the final destruction of that people by the Romans, in which it had a complete accomplishment, and the effects of it that people and that land remain under to this day. <div eID="gen15596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15597" type="x-p"/> 4. That yet a remnant should be reserved to be the monuments of mercy, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">v. 13</reference>. There was a remnant reserved in the last destruction of the Jewish nation (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Rom. xi. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">At this present time there is a remnant</hi>); for so it was written here: <hi type="italic">But in it shall be a tenth,</hi> a certain number, but a very small number in comparison with the multitude that shall perish in their unbelief. It is that which, under the law, was God's proportion; they shall be consecrated to God as the tithes were, and shall be for his service and honour. Concerning this tithe, this saved remnant, we are here told, (1.) That they shall return (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">ch. vi. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.21">x. 21</reference>), shall return from sin to God and duty, shall return out of captivity to their own land. God will turn them, and they shall be turned. (2.) That they shall be eaten, that is, shall be accepted of God as the tithe was, which was meat in God's house, <reference osisRef="Mal.3.10">Mal. iii. 10</reference>. The saving of this remnant shall be meat to the faith and hope of those that wish well to God's kingdom. (3.) That they shall be like a timber-tree in winter, which has life, though it has no leaves: <hi type="italic">As a teil-tree and as an oak, whose substance is in them even when they cast their leaves,</hi> so this remnant, though they may be stripped of their outward prosperity and share with others in common calamities, shall yet recover themselves, as a tree in the spring, and flourish again; though they fall, they shall not be utterly cast down. <hi type="italic">There is hope of a tree, though it be cut down, that it will sprout again,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.14.7">Job xiv. 7</reference>. (4.) That this distinguished remnant shall be the stay and support of the public interests. <hi type="italic">The holy seed</hi> in the soul is the substance of the man; a principle of grace reigning in the heart will keep life there; he that is <hi type="italic">born of God</hi> has <hi type="italic">his seed remaining in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.9">1 John iii. 9</reference>. So the holy seed in the land is the substance of the land, keeps it from being quite dissolved, <hi type="italic">and bears up the pillars of it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.75.3">Ps. lxxv. 3</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Isa.1.9">ch. i. 9</reference>. Some read the foregoing clause with this, thus: <hi type="italic">As the support at Shallecheth is in the elms and the oaks, so the holy seed is the substance thereof;</hi> as the trees that grow on either side of the causeway (the raised way, or terrace-walk, that leads from the king's palace to the temple, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.5">1 Kings x. 5</reference>, at the gate of Shallecheth, <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.16">1 Chron. xxvi. 16</reference>) support the causeway by keeping up the earth, which would otherwise be crumbling away, so the small residue of religious, serious, praying people, are the support of the state, and help to keep things together and save them from going to decay. Some make the holy seed to be Christ. The Jewish nation was <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> saved from utter ruin because <hi type="italic">out of it, as concerning the flesh, Christ</hi> was to come, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.5">Rom. ix. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Destroy it not, for that blessing is in it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.8">ch. lxv. 8</reference>); and when that blessing had come, it was soon destroyed. Now the consideration of this is designed for the support of the prophet in his work. Though far the greater part should perish in their unbelief, yet to some his word should be a savour of life unto life. Ministers do not wholly lose their labour if they be but instrumental to save one poor soul.  <chapter eID="Isa.6"/> <div eID="gen15597" type="x-p"/>

entries.f164cac3ea2444b03165cbf1ecddd4724c7fa610: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8418"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.13">Is 6:1-13</reference>. Vision of Jehovah in His Temple.</title> <div sID="gen13542" type="x-p"/> Isaiah is outside, near the altar in front of the temple. The doors are supposed to open, and the veil hiding the Holy of Holies to be withdrawn, unfolding to his view a vision of God represented as an Eastern monarch, attended by seraphim as His ministers of state (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.19">1Ki 22:19</reference>), and with a robe and flowing train (a badge of dignity in the East), which filled the temple. This assertion that he had seen God was, according to tradition (not sanctioned by <reference osisRef="Isa.1.1">Is 1:1</reference>; see Introduction), the pretext for sawing him asunder in Manasseh's reign (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.37">He 11:37</reference>). Visions often occur in the other prophets: in Isaiah there is only this one, and it is marked by characteristic clearness and simplicity.<div eID="gen13542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13543" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8418"/><hi type="bold">1. In ... year ... Uzziah died--</hi>Either literal death, or civil when he ceased as a leper to exercise his functions as king [Chaldee], (2Ch 26:19-21). 754 B.C. [Calmet] 758 (Common Chronology). This is not the first beginning of Isaiah's prophecies, but his inauguration to a higher degree of the prophetic office: <reference osisRef="Isa.6.9">Is 6:9</reference>, &c., implies the tone of one who had already experience of the people's obstinacy.<div eID="gen13543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13544" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord--</hi>here Adonai, Jehovah in <reference osisRef="Isa.6.5">Is 6:5</reference>; Jesus Christ is meant as speaking in <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">Is 6:10</reference>, according to <reference osisRef="John.12.41">Joh 12:41</reference>. Isaiah could only have "seen" the Son, not the divine essence (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>). The words in <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">Is 6:10</reference> are attributed by Paul (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.25">Ac 28:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.28.26">26</reference>) to the Holy Ghost. Thus the Trinity in unity is implied; as also by the thrice "Holy" (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.3">Is 6:3</reference>). Isaiah mentions the robes, temple, and seraphim, but not the form of God Himself. Whatever it was, it was different from the usual Shekinah: that was on the mercy seat, this on a throne; that a cloud and fire, of this no form is specified: over that were the cherubim, over this the seraphim; that had no clothing, this had a flowing robe and train. <div eID="gen13544" type="x-p"/>
entries.717a943b2a754005d0fdaa74c63effbaff380366: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8419"/><div sID="gen13545" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8419"/><hi type="bold">2. stood--</hi>not necessarily the posture of standing; rather, were in attendance on Him [Maurer], hovering on expanded wings.<div eID="gen13545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the--</hi>not in the Hebrew.<div eID="gen13546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13547" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seraphim--</hi>nowhere else applied to God's attendant angels; but to the fiery flying (not winged, but rapidly moving) serpents, which bit the Israelites (<reference osisRef="Num.21.6">Nu 21:6</reference>), called so from the poisonous inflammation caused by their bites. Seraph is to burn; implying the burning zeal, dazzling brightness (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.11">2Ki 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.17">6:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.13">Eze 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.3">Mt 28:3</reference>) and serpent-like rapidity of the seraphim in God's service. Perhaps Satan's form as a serpent (nachash) in his appearance to man has some connection with his original form as a seraph of light. The head of the serpent was the symbol of wisdom in Egypt (compare <reference osisRef="Num.21.8">Nu 21:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.4">2Ki 18:4</reference>). The seraphim, with six wings and one face, can hardly be identified with the cherubim, which had four wings (in the temple only two) and four faces (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.5-Ezek.1.12">Eze 1:5-12</reference>). (But compare <reference osisRef="Rev.4.8">Re 4:8</reference>). The "face" and "feet" imply a human form; something of a serpentine form (perhaps a basilisk's head, as in the temples of Thebes) may have been mixed with it: so the cherub was compounded of various animal forms. However, seraph may come from a root meaning "princely," applied in <reference osisRef="Dan.10.13">Da 10:13</reference> to Michael [Maurer]; just as cherub comes from a root (changing m into b), meaning "noble."<div eID="gen13547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">twain--</hi>Two wings alone of the six were kept ready for instant flight in God's service; two veiled their faces as unworthy to look on the holy God, or pry into His secret counsels which they fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.6">Ex 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job 4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.15">15:15</reference>); two covered their feet, or rather the whole of the lower parts of their persons--a practice usual in the presence of Eastern monarchs, in token of reverence (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.11">Eze 1:11</reference>, their bodies). Man's service a fortiori consists in reverent waiting on, still more than in active service for, God. <div eID="gen13548" type="x-p"/>
entries.261d1ebca80d1a1f6fce3ebc7a2082c48f95d501: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8420"/><div sID="gen13549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8420"/>3. (<reference osisRef="Rev.4.8">Re 4:8</reference>). The Trinity is implied (on "Lord," see on <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">Is 6:1</reference>). God's holiness is the keynote of Isaiah's whole prophecies.<div eID="gen13549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whole earth--</hi>the Hebrew more emphatically, the fulness of the whole earth is His glory (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.1">Psa 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.19">72:19</reference>). <div eID="gen13550" type="x-p"/>
entries.4462e05ba518bf4aa5530e04c6d6dc63b015bc92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8421"/><div sID="gen13551" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8421"/><hi type="bold">4. posts of ... door--</hi>rather, foundations of the thresholds.<div eID="gen13551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13552" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">house--</hi>temple.<div eID="gen13552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">smoke--</hi>the Shekinah cloud (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.10">1Ki 8:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.4">Eze 10:4</reference>). <div eID="gen13553" type="x-p"/>
entries.a200af7b8e1271065ce579f9ae30850a1f1aa47e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8422"/><div sID="gen13554" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8422"/><hi type="bold">5. undone--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.33.20">Ex 33:20</reference>). The same effect was produced on others by the presence of God (<reference osisRef="Judg.6.22">Jud 6:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.13.22">13:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.42.5">Job 42:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.42.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.5.8">Lu 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.17">Re 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen13554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13555" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lips--</hi>appropriate to the context which describes the praises of the lips, sung in alternate responses (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.20">Ex 15:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.6.3">Is 6:3</reference>) by the seraphim: also appropriate to the office of speaking as the prophet of God, about to be committed to Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.9">Is 6:9</reference>).<div eID="gen13555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13556" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seen--</hi>not strictly Jehovah Himself (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.16">1Ti 6:16</reference>), but the symbol of His presence.<div eID="gen13556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13557" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord--</hi>Hebrew, "Jehovah." <div eID="gen13557" type="x-p"/>
entries.6854c5c0aedecbd35a60aaaba96ba05bca7037f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8423"/><div sID="gen13558" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8423"/><hi type="bold">6. unto me--</hi>The seraph had been in the temple, Isaiah outside of it.<div eID="gen13558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13559" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">live coal--</hi>literally, "a hot stone," used, as in some countries in our days, to roast meat with, for example, the meat of the sacrifices. Fire was a symbol of purification, as it takes the dross out of metals (Mal 3:2, 3).<div eID="gen13559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13560" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the altar--</hi>of burnt offering, in the court of the priests before the temple. The fire on it was at first kindled by God (<reference osisRef="Lev.9.24">Le 9:24</reference>), and was kept continually burning. <div eID="gen13560" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ea2884ee0e1dcf69a77ec274459ddb303679069: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8424"/><div sID="gen13561" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8424"/><hi type="bold">7. mouth ... lips--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.6.5">Is 6:5</reference>). The mouth was touched because it was the part to be used by the prophet when inaugurated. So "tongues of fire" rested on the disciples (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.3">Ac 2:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.4">4</reference>) when they were being set apart to speak in various languages of Jesus.<div eID="gen13561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13562" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">iniquity--</hi>conscious unworthiness of acting as God's messenger.<div eID="gen13562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13563" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purged--</hi>literally, "covered," that is, expiated, not by any physical effect of fire to cleanse from sin, but in relation to the altar sacrifices, of which Messiah, who here commissions Isaiah, was in His death to be the antitype: it is implied hereby that it is only by sacrifice sin can be pardoned. <div eID="gen13563" type="x-p"/>
entries.1732f6fc471d70d4f36e497ba5a707cafa34aa55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8425"/><div sID="gen13564" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8425"/><hi type="bold">8. I ... us--</hi>The change of number indicates the Trinity (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.1.26">Ge 1:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.7">11:7</reference>). Though not a sure argument for the doctrine, for the plural may indicate merely majesty, it accords with that truth proved elsewhere.<div eID="gen13564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13565" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Whom ... who--</hi>implying that few would be willing to bear the self-denial which the delivering of such an unwelcome message to the Jews would require on the part of the messenger (compare <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.5">1Ch 29:5</reference>).<div eID="gen13565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13566" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Here am I--</hi>prompt zeal, now that he has been specially qualified for it (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.7">Is 6:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.10">1Sa 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.9.6">Ac 9:6</reference>). <div eID="gen13566" type="x-p"/>
entries.255e1fdda350b84403c15404a51bf9bb7e911d99: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8426"/><div sID="gen13567" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8426"/><hi type="bold">9. Hear ... indeed--</hi>Hebrew, "In hearing hear," that is, Though ye hear the prophet's warnings again and again, ye are doomed, because of your perverse will (<reference osisRef="John.7.17">Joh 7:17</reference>), not to understand. Light enough is given in revelation to guide those sincerely seeking to know, in order that they may do, God's will; darkness enough is left to confound the wilfully blind (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.8">Is 43:8</reference>). So in Jesus' use of parables (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.14">Mt 13:14</reference>).<div eID="gen13567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13568" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">see ... indeed--</hi>rather, "though ye see again and again," yet, &c. <div eID="gen13568" type="x-p"/>
entries.56e7ff1f108310b5a016014037a3a5111e7e0508: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8427"/><div sID="gen13569" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8427"/><hi type="bold">10. Make ... fat--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.119.17">Psa 119:17</reference>). "Render them the more hardened by thy warnings" [Maurer]. This effect is the fruit, not of the truth in itself, but of the corrupt state of their hearts, to which God here judicially gives them over (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.17">Is 63:17</reference>). Gesenius takes the imperatives as futures. "Proclaim truths, the result of which proclamation will be their becoming the more hardened" (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">Ro 1:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Ep 4:18</reference>); but this does not so well as the former set forth God as designedly giving up sinners to judicial hardening (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.8">Ro 11:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.11">2Th 2:11</reference>). In the first member of the sentence, the order is, the heart, ears, eyes; in the latter, the reverse order, the eyes, ears, heart. It is from the heart that corruption flows into the ears and eyes (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.21">Mr 7:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.22">22</reference>); but through the eyes and ears healing reaches the heart (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.17">Ro 10:17</reference>), [Bengel]. (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.21">Jr 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.2">Eze 12:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.7.11">Zec 7:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.57">Ac 7:57</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.4">2Ti 4:4</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Matt.13.15">Mt 13:15</reference>, the words are quoted in the indicative, "is waxed gross" (so the Septuagint), not the imperative, "make fat"; God's word as to the future is as certain as if it were already fulfilled. To see with one's eyes will not convince a will that is opposed to the truth (compare <reference osisRef="John.11.45">Joh 11:45</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.11.46">46</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.10">12:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.12.11">11</reference>). "One must love divine things in order to understand them" [Pascal].<div eID="gen13569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13570" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be healed--</hi>of their spiritual malady, sin (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Is 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.3">Psa 103:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.14">Jr 17:14</reference>). <div eID="gen13570" type="x-p"/>
entries.692c85dd71f174849d8a7d882fbdb0b851dd5371: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8428"/><div sID="gen13571" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8428"/><hi type="bold">11. how long--</hi>will this wretched condition of the nation being hardened to its destruction continue?<div eID="gen13571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">until--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.5.9">Is 5:9</reference>)--fulfilled primarily at the Babylonish captivity, and more fully at the dispersion under the Roman Titus. <div eID="gen13572" type="x-p"/>
entries.3101b7d877870cf0b33a41fd5412c50d0a7c0d76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8429"/><div sID="gen13573" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8429"/>12. (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.21">2Ki 25:21</reference>).<div eID="gen13573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13574" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forsaking--</hi>abandonment of dwellings by their inhabitants (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.29">Jr 4:29</reference>). <div eID="gen13574" type="x-p"/>
entries.40f9a302f79b2c9b8ed2423192a3b2d4df4341c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8430"/><div sID="gen13575" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8430"/><hi type="bold">13. and it shall return, and ... be eaten--</hi>Rather, "but it shall be again given over to be consumed": if even a tenth survive the first destruction, it shall be destroyed by a second (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.25">Is 5:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.1-Ezek.5.12">Eze 5:1-5, 12</reference>), [Maurer and Horsley]. In English Version, "return" refers to the poor remnant left in the land at the Babylonish captivity (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.14">2Ki 24:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.12">25:12</reference>), which afterwards fled to Egypt in fear (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.26">2Ki 25:26</reference>), and subsequently returned thence along with others who had fled to Moab and Edom (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.11">Jr 40:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.40.12">12</reference>), and suffered under further divine judgments.<div eID="gen13575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13576" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tell--</hi>rather, "terebinth" or "turpentine tree" (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Is 1:29</reference>).<div eID="gen13576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13577" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">substance ... when ... cast ... leaves--</hi>rather, "As a terebinth or oak in which, when they are cast down (not 'cast their leaves,' <reference osisRef="Job.14.7">Job 14:7</reference>), the trunk or stock remains, so the holy seed (<reference osisRef="Ezra.9.2">Ezr 9:2</reference>) shall be the stock of that land." The seeds of vitality still exist in both the land and the scattered people of Judea, waiting for the returning spring of God's favor (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Ro 11:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.23-Rom.11.29">23-29</reference>). According to Isaiah, not all Israel, but the elect remnant alone, is destined to salvation. God shows unchangeable severity towards sin, but covenant faithfulness in preserving a remnant, and to it Isaiah bequeaths the prophetic legacy of the second part of his book (the fortieth through sixty-sixth chapters). <chapter eID="Isa.6"/>

entries.d917db88bb5f44e2f3ad9f787e75fd46d91d03a8: <div eID="gen26789" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen26790" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26791" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26791" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26790" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26792" type="x-p"/> This chapter, by a particular designation of Isaiah to the prophetic office, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.8">Isa 6:1-8</reference>, introduces, with great solemnity, a declaration of the whole tenor of the Diving conduct in reference to his people, who, on account of their unbelief and impenitence, should for a very long period be given up to a judicial blindness and hardness of heart, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.9">Isa 6:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">Isa 6:10</reference>; and visited with such calamities as would issue on the total desolation of their country, and their general dispersion, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.11">Isa 6:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.12">Isa 6:12</reference>. The prophet adds, however, that under their repeated dispersions, (by the Chaldeans, Romans, etc.), a small remnant would be preserved as a seed from which will be raised a people, in whom will be fulfilled all the Divine promises, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">Isa 6:13</reference>. <div eID="gen26792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26793" type="x-p"/> As this vision seems to contain a solemn designation of Isaiah to the prophetic office, it is by most interpreters thought to be the first in order of his prophecies. But this perhaps may not be so; for Isaiah is said, in the general title of his prophecies, to have prophesied in the time of Uzziah, whose acts, first and last, he wrote, <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.22">2Chr 26:22</reference>; which is usually done by a contemporary prophet; and the phrase, in the year that Uzziah died, probably means after the death of Uzziah; as the same phrase (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.28">Isa 14:28</reference>) means after the death of Ahaz. Not that Isaiah's prophecies are placed in exact order of time. Chapters 2, 3, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.1-Isa.4.6">Isa 4:1-6</reference>, 5, seem by internal marks to be antecedent to chap. 1; they suit the time of Uzziah, or the former part of Jotham's reign; whereas chap. 1 can hardly be earlier than the last years of Jotham. See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.1.7">Isa 1:7</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.2.1">Isa 2:1</reference> (note). This might be a new designation, to introduce more solemnly a general dedication of the whole course of God's dispensations in regard to his people and the fates of the nation; which are even now still depending, and will not be fully accomplished till the final restoration of Israel. <div eID="gen26793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26794" type="x-p"/> In this vision the ideas are taken in general from royal majesty, as displayed by the monarchs of the East; for the prophet could not represent the ineffable presence of God by any other than sensible and earthly images. The particular scenery of it is taken from the temple. God is represented as seated on his throne above the ark, in the most holy place, where the glory appeared above the cherubim, surrounded by his attendant ministers. This is called by God himself "the place of his throne, and the place of the soles of his feet," <reference osisRef="Eze.43.7">Eze 43:7</reference>. "A glorious throne exalted of old, is the place of our sanctuary," saith the prophet Jeremiah, chap, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.12">Jer 17:12</reference>. The very posture of sitting is a mark of state and solemnity: Sed et ipsum verbum sedere regni significat potestatem, saith Jerome, Comment. in <reference osisRef="Eph.1.20">Eph 1:20</reference>. See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.3.1">Isa 3:1</reference> (note). St. John, who has taken many sublime images from the prophets of the Old Testament, and in particular from Isaiah, hath exhibited the same scenery, drawn out into a greater number of particulars; <reference osisRef="Rev.4.1-Rev.4.11">Rev 4:1-11</reference>. <div eID="gen26794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26795" type="x-p"/> The veil, separating the most holy place from the holy or outermost part of the temple, is here supposed to be taken away; for the prophet, to whom the whole is exhibited, is manifestly placed by the altar of burnt-offering, at the entrance of the temple, (compare <reference osisRef="Eze.43.5">Eze 43:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.43.6">Eze 43:6</reference>), which was filled with the train of the robe, the spreading and overflowing of the Divine glory. The Lord upon the throne, according to St. John (<reference osisRef="Joh.12.41">Joh 12:41</reference>), was Christ; and the vision related to his future kingdom when the veil of separation was to be removed, and the whole earth was to be filled with the glory of God, revealed to all mankind: which is likewise implied in the hymn of the seraphim, the design of which is, saith Jerome on the place, Ut mysterium Trinitatis in una Divinitate demonstrent; et nequaquam templum Judaicum, sicut prius, sed omnem terram illius gloria plenam esse testentur; "That they may point out the mystery of the Trinity in one Godhead; and that the Jewish temple alone should not be, as formerly, the place of the Divine glory, for the whole earth should be filled with it." It relates, indeed, primarily to the prophet's own time, and the obduration of the Jews of that age, and their punishment by the Babylonish captivity; but extends in its full attitude to the age of Messiah, and the blindness of the Jews to the Gospel, (see <reference osisRef="Mat.13.14">Mat 13:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.12.40">Joh 12:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.28.26">Act 28:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.8">Rom 11:8</reference>), the desolation of their country by the Romans, and their being rejected by God. That nevertheless a holy seed - a remnant, should be preserved; and that the nation should spread out and flourish again from the old stock. - L. <div eID="gen26795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26796" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen26796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26797" type="x-p"/> The Lord - Fifty-one MSS. of Kennicott's, and fifty-four of De Rossi's, and one edition; in the 8th verse, (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.8">Isa 6:8</reference>); forty-four MSS. of Kennicott's, and forty-six of De Rossi's, and one edition; and in the 11th verse (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.11">Isa 6:11</reference>); thirty-three MSS. of Kennicott's, and many of De Rossi's, and one edition, for אדני Adonai, "the Lord" read יהוה "Jehovah," which is probably the true reading; (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.6.6">Isa 6:6</reference>); as in many other places, in which the superstition of the Jews has substituted אדני Adonai for יהוה Yehovah. One of my own MSS., a very ancient and large folio, to which the points and the masora have been added by a later hand, has יהוה Yehovah in the 1st and 8th verses, in the teeth of the masora, which orders it in both places to be read אדני Adonai.
entries.a67dedf144e5ccf1382d534abc3113a9a1eb0b4a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen26797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26798" type="x-p"/> Above it stood the seraphim - שרפים seraphim, from שרף seraph, to burn. He saw says Kimchi, the angels as flames of fire, that the depravity of that generation might be exhibited, which was worthy of being totally burnt up. <div eID="gen26798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26799" type="x-p"/> He covered his feet "He covereth his feet" - By the feet the Hebrews mean all the lower parts of the body. But the people of the East generally wearing long robes, reaching to the ground, and covering the lower parts of the body down to the feet, it may hence have been thought want of respect and decency to appear in public and on solemn occasions with even the feet themselves uncovered. Kempfer, speaking of the king of Persia giving audience, says, Rex in medio supremi atrii cruribus more patrio inflexis sedebat: corpus tunica investiebat flava, ad suras cum staret protensa; discumbentis vero pedes discalceatos pro urbanitate patria operiens. - Amoen. Exot. p. 227. "The king sat on the floor cross-legged, as is the custom of the country. He was covered with a yellow garment, which reached down to the feet when standing, but covered the feet for decency when sitting with his slippers off." Sir John Chardin's MS. note on this place of Isaiah is as follows: Grande marque de respect en orient de se cacher les pieds, quand on est assis, et de baisser le visage. Quand le souvrain se monstre en Chine et a Japon, chacun se jette le visage contre terre, et il n'est pas permis de regarder le roi; "It is a great mark of respect in the East to cover the feet, and to bow down the head in the presence of the king."
entries.c16f69ee8d271b5990eb37f1cd593041964ee9d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen26799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26800" type="x-p"/> Holy, holy, holy - This hymn performed by the seraphim, divided into two choirs, the one singing responsively to the other, which Gregory Nazian., Carm. 18, very elegantly calls Συμφωνον, αντιφωνον, αγγελων στασιν, is formed upon the practice of alternate singing, which prevailed in the Jewish Church from the time of Moses, whose ode at the Red Sea was thus performed, (see <reference osisRef="Exo.15.20">Exo 15:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.15.21">Exo 15:21</reference>), to that of Ezra, under whom the priests and Levites sung alternately, "O praise Jehovah, for he is gracious; <div eID="gen26800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26801" type="x-p"/> For his mercy endureth for ever;" <reference osisRef="Ezr.3.11">Ezr 3:11</reference>. See De Sac. Poes. Hebr. Prael. xix., at the beginning.
entries.3221d22b97826559cfebb8691f8ad529f2a39a95: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen26801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26802" type="x-p"/> Wo is me! for I am undone - נדמיתי nidmeythi, I am become dumb. There is something exceedingly affecting in this complaint. I am a man of unclean lips; I cannot say, Holy, holy, holy! which the seraphs exclaim. They are holy; I am not so: they see God, and live; I have seen him, and must die, because I am unholy. Only the pure in heart shall see God; and they only can live in his presence for ever, Reader, lay this to heart; and instead of boasting of thy excellence, and trusting in thy might, or comforting thyself in thy comparative innocence, thou wilt also be dumb before him, because thou hast been a man of unclean lips, and because thou hast still an unclean heart. <div eID="gen26802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26803" type="x-p"/> I am undone "I am struck dumb" - נדמיתי nidmeythi, twenty-eight MSS. (five ancient) and three editions. - I understand it as from דום dum or דמם damam, silere, "to be silent;" and so it is rendered by the Syriac, Vulgate, Symmachus, and by some of the Jewish interpreters, apud Sal. b. Melec. The rendering of the Syriac is תויר אני tavir ani, stupens, attonitus sum, "I am amazed." He immediately gives the reason why he was struck dumb: because he was a man of polluted lips, and dwelt among a people of polluted lips, and was unworthy, either to join the seraphim in singing praises to God, or to be the messenger of God to his people. Compare <reference osisRef="Exo.4.10">Exo 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.6.12">Exo 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.1.6">Jer 1:6</reference>.
entries.abe91730a9bd4efcccf98430a868903f644dc674: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen26803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26804" type="x-p"/> A live coal - The word of prophecy, which was put into the mouth of the prophet. <div eID="gen26804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26805" type="x-p"/> From off the altar - That is, from the altar of burnt-offerings, before the door of the temple, on which the fire that came down at first from heaven (<reference osisRef="Lev.9.24">Lev 9:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.1">2Chr 7:1</reference>) was perpetually burning. It was never to be extinguished, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.12">Lev 6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.13">Lev 6:13</reference>.
entries.0718efb312bcccf834b69299fab93d085ed9e290: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen26805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26806" type="x-p"/> And he said - לי li, to me, two MSS. and the Syriac. Thirteen MSS. have ראה raah, in the regular form.
entries.e05e6b5ce7d58a436d225c51508a9a3187e4d393: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen26806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26807" type="x-p"/> Make the heart of this people fat "Gross" - The prophet speaks of the event, the fact as it would actually happen, not of God's purpose and act by his ministry. The prophets are in other places said to perform the thing which they only foretell: - "Lo! I have given thee a charge this day <div eID="gen26807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26808" type="x-p"/> Over the nations, and over the kingdoms; <div eID="gen26808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26809" type="x-p"/> To pluck up, and to pull down; <div eID="gen26809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26810" type="x-p"/> To destroy, and to demolish; <div eID="gen26810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26811" type="x-p"/> To build, and to plant." <reference osisRef="Jer.1.10">Jer 1:10</reference>. <div eID="gen26811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26812" type="x-p"/> And Ezekiel says, "When I came to destroy the city," that is, as it is rendered in the margin of our version, "when I came to prophesy that the city should be destroyed;" <reference osisRef="Eze.43.3">Eze 43:3</reference>. To hear, and not understand; to see, and not perceive; is a common saying in many languages. Demosthenes uses it, and expressly calls it a proverb: ὡστε το της παροιμιας ὁρωντας μη ὁρᾳν, και ακουοντας μη ακουειν; Conttra Aristogit. I., sub fin. The prophet, by the bold figure in the sentiment above mentioned, and the elegant form and construction of the sentence, has raised it from a common proverb into a beautiful mashal, and given it the sublime air of poetry. <div eID="gen26812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26813" type="x-p"/> Or the words may be understood thus, according to the Hebrew idiom: "Ye certainly hear, but do not understand; ye certainly see, but do not acknowledge." Seeing this is the case, make the heart of this people fat - declare it to be stupid and senseless; and remove from them the means of salvation, which they have so long abused. <div eID="gen26813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26814" type="x-p"/> There is a saying precisely like this in Aeschylus: - - - - βλεποντες εβλεπον ματην, Κλυοντες ουκ ηκουον. <div eID="gen26814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26815" type="x-p"/> Aesch. Prom. Vinct. 456. "Seeing, they saw in vain; and hearing, they did not understand." <div eID="gen26815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26816" type="x-p"/> And shut "Close up" - השע hasha. This word Sal. ben Melec explains to this sense, in which it is hardly used elsewhere, on the authority of Onkelos. He says it means closing up the eyes, so that one cannot see; that the root is שוע shava, by which word the Targum has rendered the word טח tach, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.42">Lev 14:42</reference>, וטח את בית vetach eth beith, "and shall plaster the house." And the word טח tach is used in the same sense, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.18">Isa 44:18</reference>. So that it signifies to close up the eyes by some matter spread upon the lids. Mr. Harmer very ingeniously applies to this passage a practice of sealing up the eyes as a ceremony, or as a kind of punishment used in the East, from which the image may possibly be taken. Observ. 2:278. <div eID="gen26816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26817" type="x-p"/> With their heart "With their hearts" - ובלבבו ubilebabo, fifteen MSS. of Kennicott's and fourteen of De Rossi's, and two editions, with the Septuagint, Syriac, Chaldee, and Vulgate. <div eID="gen26817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26818" type="x-p"/> And be healed "And I should heal" - ואר פא veer pa, Septuagint, Vulgate. So likewise <reference osisRef="Mat.13.14">Mat 13:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.12.40">Joh 12:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.28.27">Act 28:27</reference>.
entries.47d343201a3ac2f932d7b73afb182b2d890a19ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen26818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26819" type="x-p"/> Be utterly desolate "Be left" - For תשאה tishaeh, the Septuagint and Vulgate read תשאר tishshaer.
entries.fdfb4c0862ec9a0bca28e26724bfb439d3e73aa5: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen26819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26820" type="x-p"/> A tenth - This passage, though somewhat obscure, and variously explained by various interpreters, has, I think, been made so clear by the accomplishment of the prophecy, that there remains little room to doubt of the sense of it. When Nebuchadnezzar had carried away the greater and better part of the people into captivity, there was yet a tenth remaining in the land, the poorer sort left to be vinedressers and husbandmen, under Gedaliah, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.12">2Kgs 25:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.22">2Kgs 25:22</reference>, and the dispersed Jews gathered themselves together, and returned to him, <reference osisRef="Jer.40.12">Jer 40:12</reference>; yet even these, fleeing into Egypt after the death of Gedaliah, contrary to the warning of God given by the prophet Jeremiah, miserably perished there.
